module.title: 4 · Model fit & classification
module.summary: Judge a binary model by likelihood-based fit (pseudo-R², LR test) and by classification: turn predicted probabilities into 0/1 at a threshold, build a confusion matrix, read accuracy, and trace the threshold-free ROC curve and its AUC — all with numpy, no sklearn.

stages.title: Two ways to ask 'is it any good?'
stages.html:
Fit versus classification

There is no ordinary R² in MLE land. statsmodels reports McFadden's Pseudo R² = 1 − ℓ(model)/ℓ(null), comparing the fitted log-likelihood to a null model with only an intercept. Values of 0.2–0.4 already indicate a strong fit — do not expect the 0.9 you might see in OLS. The LLR p-value is a likelihood-ratio test that all slopes are jointly zero (the binary analogue of the overall F-test).

From probabilities to decisions

To actually classify, pick a threshold (commonly 0.5) and predict ŷ = 1 when p̂ ≥ threshold. Cross-tabulate against the truth to get the confusion matrix:

  • TP true positives, TN true negatives — correct calls.
  • FP false positives (predicted 1, actually 0), FN false negatives (predicted 0, actually 1) — the two error types.

accuracy = (TP + TN) / n

Key idea. Pseudo-R² and the LR test grade the probabilities; the confusion matrix and accuracy grade the 0/1 decisions at a chosen threshold.

stages.title: Why one threshold is not enough: ROC & AUC
stages.html:
Accuracy can lie

If 90% of cases are y = 0, a lazy model that always predicts 0 scores 90% accuracy while catching zero positives. With imbalance you need to look at both error types and to vary the threshold.

The ROC curve

Sweep the threshold from 1 down to 0. At each one record the true-positive rate TPR = TP/(all actual 1s) and the false-positive rate FPR = FP/(all actual 0s). Plotting TPR against FPR traces the ROC curve. A perfect model hugs the top-left corner; random guessing is the 45° diagonal.

The area under that curve, the AUC, summarises ranking quality in one number: it equals the probability that a randomly chosen positive gets a higher p̂ than a randomly chosen negative. AUC = 0.5 is coin-flipping; AUC = 1.0 is perfect separation; 0.8+ is generally strong. AUC is threshold-free, so it judges the probabilities themselves rather than one cut-off.

Key idea. AUC measures how well the model ranks positives above negatives, independent of any threshold — robust even when classes are imbalanced.

stages.title: Confusion matrix, accuracy, and a hand-rolled ROC/AUC
stages.note: Pure numpy: threshold predicted probabilities at 0.5 for the confusion matrix and accuracy, then sweep all thresholds to build the ROC curve and integrate it with the trapezoid rule (no sklearn, no np.trapz).
stages.code:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 800
x1 = rng.normal(0, 1, n); x2 = rng.normal(0, 1, n)
eta = -0.3 + 1.5*x1 - 0.8*x2
p = 1/(1+np.exp(-eta)); y = rng.binomial(1, p)
df = pd.DataFrame({'y': y, 'x1': x1, 'x2': x2})
res = smf.logit('y ~ x1 + x2', df).fit(disp=0)

y = df['y'].to_numpy()
phat = res.predict(df).to_numpy()
yhat = (phat >= 0.5).astype(int)
TP = int(((yhat==1)&(y==1)).sum()); TN = int(((yhat==0)&(y==0)).sum())
FP = int(((yhat==1)&(y==0)).sum()); FN = int(((yhat==0)&(y==1)).sum())
acc = (TP+TN)/n
print('Pseudo R-squared: %.3f' % res.prsquared)
print('Confusion matrix (rows=actual, cols=predicted):')
print('            pred 0   pred 1')
print('actual 0   %6d   %6d' % (TN, FP))
print('actual 1   %6d   %6d' % (FN, TP))
print('Accuracy @0.5: %.3f' % acc)

P = (y==1).sum(); N = (y==0).sum()
thr = np.linspace(0, 1, 201)
tpr = np.array([((phat>=t)&(y==1)).sum()/P for t in thr])
fpr = np.array([((phat>=t)&(y==0)).sum()/N for t in thr])
order = np.argsort(fpr); fs = fpr[order]; ts = tpr[order]
auc = float(np.sum((fs[1:]-fs[:-1])*(ts[1:]+ts[:-1])/2))   # trapezoid
print('AUC: %.3f' % auc)

plt.figure(figsize=(6,3.7))
plt.plot(fpr, tpr, color='#da9100', lw=2.2, label='ROC (AUC=%.3f)' % auc)
plt.plot([0,1],[0,1], color='#6f6b57', lw=1, ls='--', label='random')
plt.xlabel('False positive rate'); plt.ylabel('True positive rate')
plt.title('ROC curve   accuracy@0.5=%.3f' % acc)
plt.legend(loc='lower right', fontsize=8)

stages.title: Move the threshold, trade off the two errors
stages.note: Slide the decision threshold. Raising it makes the model more conservative about predicting 1: false positives fall but false negatives rise. Accuracy is one summary of that trade-off — and its best value is rarely exactly at 0.5.
stages.template:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 800
x1 = rng.normal(0, 1, n); x2 = rng.normal(0, 1, n)
eta = -0.3 + 1.5*x1 - 0.8*x2
p = 1/(1+np.exp(-eta)); y = rng.binomial(1, p)
df = pd.DataFrame({'y': y, 'x1': x1, 'x2': x2})
res = smf.logit('y ~ x1 + x2', df).fit(disp=0)
y = df['y'].to_numpy(); phat = res.predict(df).to_numpy()
t = {{thresh}}
yhat = (phat >= t).astype(int)
TP = int(((yhat==1)&(y==1)).sum()); TN = int(((yhat==0)&(y==0)).sum())
FP = int(((yhat==1)&(y==0)).sum()); FN = int(((yhat==0)&(y==1)).sum())
acc = (TP+TN)/n
plt.figure(figsize=(6,3.7))
bars = plt.bar(['TP','TN','FP','FN'], [TP,TN,FP,FN],
               color=['#da9100','#af983f','#6f6b57','#c9c6ac'])
for b,v in zip(bars,[TP,TN,FP,FN]):
    plt.text(b.get_x()+b.get_width()/2, v+4, str(v), ha='center', fontsize=9)
plt.ylabel('count')
plt.title('threshold=%.2f   accuracy=%.3f   (FP=%d, FN=%d)' % (t, acc, FP, FN))

stages.title: Check
stages.prompt: A dataset is 95% zeros. A model that predicts 0 for everyone reports 95% accuracy. What does that reveal?
choices: Accuracy alone is misleading under class imbalance; check FN/TPR and AUC
Accuracy should always be replaced by pseudo-R²
The threshold must have been set above 0.95
stages.hint: How many true positives did that model catch?
stages.explain: It catches zero positives despite 95% accuracy, so accuracy is uninformative under imbalance — threshold-free measures like the ROC/AUC and the true-positive rate expose the failure.

stages.title: Check
choices: The model ranks positives above negatives no better than random chance
Exactly half the predictions are correct
stages.hint: AUC is the probability a random positive outscores a random negative.
stages.explain: AUC = 0.5 is the diagonal of the ROC plot — the model's probability ranking is no better than a coin flip, regardless of the chosen threshold.

stages.title: Check
stages.prompt: Raising the classification threshold from 0.5 to 0.8 will generally:
choices: Increase both false positives and false negatives
Decrease false positives but increase false negatives
stages.hint: A higher bar to predict '1' makes the model more cautious about positives.
stages.explain: Demanding p̂ ≥ 0.8 makes positive predictions rarer, so false positives fall while genuine positives get missed more often, raising false negatives — the classic precision/recall trade-off.

stages.title: Does 95% accuracy mean a good model?
stages.prompt: A dataset is 95% zeros. You just saw that always predicting 0 scores 95% accuracy. Claim: that 95% accuracy shows the classifier is performing well.
stages.hint: How many actual positives does the all-zeros rule catch? Think about the true-positive rate and the AUC, not raw accuracy.
stages.explain: This is the accuracy-under-imbalance trap. A model that predicts 0 for everyone catches ZERO positives yet still scores 95% — accuracy just echoes the base rate when classes are imbalanced. Judge such a model by threshold-free, ranking measures: the true-positive rate and the ROC AUC (0.5 = no better than chance here). Boundary: accuracy is informative only when the classes are roughly balanced and the costs of the two error types are similar; otherwise lean on AUC, precision/recall, or a cost-weighted threshold.
